utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please give me a clarification on a question that was asked by the Defence. I thought I understood that the Defence was interested in finding out your opinion or your view as an expert in the matter of the rates, death rates, in normal times, in normal circumstances, and how much was it higher or lower or the same, in comparison to what happened in the period between summer 1992 and summer 1994? I didn't quite follow your answer so I would be grateful for it now.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for this question. We presented a comparison of this type in our report. And please if you could refer to section in which the rates are discussed, I am speaking about page 40 and page 42 of the report. At page 40, we present table 15. In this table, we begin our discussion by showing rates obtained for six municipalities relevant to this discussion in this report for two periods. One is the year 1991, just one single year. And this is the column titled "death rate 1991." At the bottom of this column, we see the death rate presented for six municipalities together it is 676,2 deaths per 100.000 population. This is how we should read this rate. And next to it we have death rate shown for the two-year period for the year 1990 and 1991. This period is directly comparable in terms of its length with the indictment period, which is approximately two years, too. The two-year rate equals 1.342,23 deaths per 100.000 population. In table 16 under -- just directly under table 15, we present rates in the first row of the table. For the killed population, natural death rate and overall death rate. Killing rate, natural death rate, and overall death rate. This rate can be directly compared with the rate for the years 1990, 1991, presented in table 15. Overall death rate is just the sum of the two, the rate of killed and the rate of natural deaths. In table 17 on page 42, we show ratios of the rates of killed and natural deaths and overall death rate. To the rate, empirical rate observed for the Sarajevo Six in 1990 and 1991. So we take the rate empirical rate for the years 1990, 1991, as a baseline standard and show, in table 17, the ratios, the difference, relative difference of the rates we obtained for the killed population and natural deaths and overall death rates, in comparison to this empirical rate. For instance, overall death rate in table 17 equal 1,65, means that the rate obtained for the years of the indictment period, the overall death rate for the indictment period, is by 65 per cent higher, by 65 per cent higher than the prewar rate for the Sarajevo Six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are still talking about the population of the same number? The same size? Normally, is there an increase in the population?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rates are relative measures which can be directly compared, the population size is the same. It is 100.000 population. Rate shows the number of events per a standard population which is 100.000 individuals. So, it is -- the size is adjusted therefore, we stress in this report, rates are the measures to compare, not absolute numbers, rates. And the rates tell us that mortality, overall mortality was higher in the indictment period, compared to prewar mortality by 65 per cent. Moreover, we see that rate for killings is higher than the rate for natural deaths in the indictment period in relative terms. So deaths, because of killing, were more frequent than deaths because of natural causes of death. And killing are generally violent deaths that would have never happened if there were no conflict in Sarajevo in this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you. I am just trying to find out whether my understanding of your page 42 of the report is correct. Am I right in understanding that the chance of being killed by the war would be for children, between zero and four years, eight times as high as the chance to die by natural causes?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, generally, this is the understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it -- is my understanding correct that if I look at the population of 0 to 17 years, well, let's say the youth, that the chance of being killed compared the chance of to die by natural causes would be 18 times as high?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it also be true that the chance of being killed for war circumstances for these category of youngsters between 0 and 17 years would be comparatively lower than such a risk for people between 18 and 69 years, that is, approximately one-third. So that young children, although they had a chance of dying because of the war circumstances which, in general, would be up to almost 20 times as high, at the same time, these children, the chance of being killed by war events would be approximately one-third of the chance of being killed, compared to, I would say, adults up to 70 years old?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I am just trying to understand the figures and see what they are all about. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are related to the questions of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they are, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The matter that we talked about, figures as such, is not something new from the Bench, but if is a specific aspect, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's new. It's new because if this witness has to bring new data, as it was suggested by His Honour Judge Nieto-Navia what are we going to do with it and when are we going to be able to question the witness? I don't know whether this data can be given now, which would be the best. That is the first question I am asking. But that is more a question for the Chamber and not the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first ask the witness, at what -- in what time she could produce the figures Judge Nieto-Navia was asking for, that is to make a distinction between those excluded for being out of the geographical area, those being excluded because being out of the time limit or both?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible to do it tomorrow. I am in court tomorrow in another case, so late in the afternoon we could provide these figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, if we first see that figures, then we will see whether there is any specific need to put additional questions to the witness. Mr. Stamp, if that would be acceptable for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, it would be. We are in the hands of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think it will take much time, but even if it would -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the methodology which goes down to two, I have two questions that arise from the questions asked by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, you said earlier that the period which was covered by the indictment, the rate, the mortality rate, increased by 65 per cent. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, compared the period 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Indeed. Now, Madam Witness, were you able to do the following, since you had the figures going from January 1992 to September 1994, were you able to examine what was the increase of the mortality rate for the three months, May, June, July, that is the three months of the beginning of the war before General Galic took over the command? Have you done this exercise, and if you haven't, could you do it and give it together with the responses that you are to give starting from tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We haven't done it, but I believe I can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it is the wish of the Defence that the, may I say, the death rates of the period covered by the indictment, would be compared with the death rate of the first month of the conflict. Then, of course, you asked some questions about that, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Would you please indicate when the conflict started or is it these three months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which area, this is also important for me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Area, within the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are still talking about the same area, since it is only about the six municipalities that we are talking about and that Madam could deal with, and I think objectively speaking, that is what she should be compared to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we are trying to find out whether the effects of the war as far as death rates were different --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... compared the later months covered by the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, we could even take the month of April, May, June and July, since we would then focus on these four months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can this be done by months or periods of three months because I can't imagine that the month of April might show a picture which might not be easy to understand. So that's your question? Is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, I apologise. There was a second question which was the following: In relation to the clarification that you have asked for, in relation to the child mortality and youth mortality, what I wanted is for the expert to have a look at page 64 of her report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Madam, so that we can understand this report as we should, the figures that we have here, and I believe that is at the end of the table, these numbers, are they years -- no, I apologise. Are these percentages, the numbers below the table?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are all absolute numbers, but the figure itself, the chart, shows percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam, as far as the 5 per cent are concerned, let us take 5 per cent on the side of men. What is the upper limit that we are unable to read in the table?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upper limit of percentage, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No. We have a column here which represents 5 per cent of men. The majority are civilians and about one-third or a smaller number are military personnel. In order to be able to understand properly, could you please tell us, what the maximum projection would be, when we are talking about the age groups on the second axis of the chart.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Age group, 10 to 19, but, please, don't mix up things again. This figure shows the structure of the sample and cannot be used in any comparisons of intensities of death or wounding. Similar figure for wounding. So this is just a structure, a structure of the sample, you know. So these are not measures of intensity of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We are talking about the same thing, but you would probably agree with me that the upper limit is 18. Allow me to put the question to you. The question is simply: Is the upper range of the second column approximately indicating up to the age of 18?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In the projection?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it is given in the table above this figure these are 10 years intervals or equal. First one is from 0 to 9. Next one is 10 to 19. Third one, 20 to 29 and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So the upper limit is 20?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the upper limit of the second interval is 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. 19. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The upper limit that you just spoke of is in respect of which table?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is page 64, table 64 -- page 64, table A3.1 in which we show in the standard demographic way the age distribution of the killed population and we show the same figures in the chart at the bottom of the page. This is A3.2. These are the same figures as in the table only shown as percentages. And the -- it is a general information about the sample and its age structure and nothing more than that. No comparisons can be made on the basis of what we see here on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words, they are just absolute numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are just absolute numbers. It is the numbers, nothing more than that, absolute numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the percentage of these --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The percentage of the particular group in the sample, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the rates -- excuse me, if you let me to finish, allow me to finish. Rates relate events in a particular age group, for instance, to the population in this particular age group, which is a different thing. Completely different thing. And this is a measure of intensity that can be compared between age groups, between populations, between countries, in time, in whatever way. That is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. In respect to age groups, you have also broken it down in table 1 to civilian casualties 10 to 17 years old, have you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. We basically have information about single years of age, we can show the distribution by any age classification that is needed. In the annexes, we use the standard demographic way of presenting our statistics. In demography we use either one year age groups, 5 year age groups or 10 year age groups. We have chosen 10 year age groups because this is a brief way of summarising age distribution of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, since I see that there are no further questions at this moment, I would like to thank you, Ms. Tabeau, but tell you at the same time, that you are not finally excused, but if the parties would like to add -- to ask questions in relation to the figures you are producing to us. And I think the most proper way of doing it, Madam Registrar, is that they will be sent to the Registry directly by you. So, we forget that you are employed by the Office of the Prosecutor, and you directly deliver your figures to the -- to the Registry. May I then also ask you, especially since this might even be for a bit longer period of time, that it was yesterday, I did not specifically ask you, but from your answers I understood that it was clear to you that you do not speak with anyone, not with colleagues, not someone with, not someone outside of the OTP about your testimony in this court and that remains valid until you will be finally excused. Thank you very much for coming and answering questions of both parties and the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, Mr. Stamp, that the Prosecution is ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Ismet Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will wait until -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know if we need to resolve the question of the documents first or should we wait until the end of the testimony of Mrs. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... do it by now. We have not yet asked the usher to bring in the witness. Madam Registrar, could you please assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3731A, addendum to Prosecutor's submission pursuant to Rule 94 bis of expert report Ewa Tabeau --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is it possible to slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of everything that relates to Mrs. Tabeau's report, perhaps we could do this after we receive the additional information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... parts. I have no objection against that. I don't know whether it makes a big difference, but if the final figures would cast in whatever way, serious doubts as to the other parts of the report but if it -- if the Defence would prefer that, okay, let's then do it this way. Then, Madam Registrar, could you please -- would the same be true for all the other documents that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think that all the other documents which do not relate to the report could be dealt with now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the issue as to the documents relevant to the report itself, I would submit that there is sufficient evidence before the Court for the Court to take that decision now, notwithstanding that she has been asked to do some follow-up calculations or research. That is not, it is my submission, a sufficient reason to prevent us from dealing with matters which have been covered sufficiently for them to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will first consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Taking into account that there might not be serious reasons, legal reasons, not to do it now. On the other hand, it might be very practical, if we're dealing with the numbers anyhow, that we do it all at the same time. So, if we say that we do it later, then this has no meaning whatsoever as far as the admissibility as such. It is just for practical reasons, and whether that would change or not, of course you would never know in advance. It is not in appreciation of the legal situation, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort the next witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration will be handed out to you by the usher, and may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. You will first be examined by counsel for it Prosecution. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hadzic. Could you start by telling us your full name.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I am Ismet Hadzic, son of Dervis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what was your occupation before the conflict broke out in Sarajevo, say in January, February, of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I worked at Energoinvest in the control of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not catch what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. You said you worked at Energoinvest and can you continue please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Energoinvest working on the jobs of control without destruction. I was a specialist for materials research, for nondestructive or nonexplosive materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you a mechanical engineer?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where did you live at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I lived in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you live alone or did you live with a family at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: After the Olympic Games in 1984, I got an apartment in Dobrinja and I lived there in the area -- in the neighbourhood of Dobrinja with my wife and three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in the course of the conflict did you have any position in relation to the parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, during the conflict, in for example, 1993, did you have any position in relation to any of the parties in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: The -- I was appointed Commander of the Dobrinja Brigade on the 6th of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Before your appointment as Commander of the Dobrinja Brigade, could you tell us briefly, if you can, or describe events which lead up to the outbreak of fighting in the area around Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: The most important things to say are that Dobrinja was closed on the 4th of May, 1992. What I mean by that is that it was blocked by checkpoints towards the city. It was isolated from the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By whom? By whom was it isolated do you know, or which group?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: By Serb forces. The Serb forces put up a checkpoint between the Olympic settlement in Mojmilo and the area of Dobrinja, they placed trucks and logs there so that was the only road that led to the city and that was closed, thereby cutting us off from the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you, apart from these checkpoints, did you observe any other movement of troops in the community before the outbreak of fighting?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1991, while the conflicts in Slovenia and Croatia were going on, large numbers of the Serb or the Yugoslav Army forces were withdrawing from those areas. So they were passing through the roads and streets of Dobrinja, which lead to Lukavica with all their soldiers and equipment. There were hundreds of tanks and APCs that arrived at the Lukavica Barracks. With the arrival of all those people, they were already coming into the Dobrinja neighbourhood and being very rowdy in the local cafes in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And before the outbreak of fighting did the civilians or the people in Dobrinja do anything or organise in any way?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I would like to say that something that made the people of Dobrinja organise themselves was the fact that the Serb forces came out to the water supplies around the Mojmilo hills. These were the water reservoirs outside of the city. This is the reservoir that supplied almost 70 per cent of the city of Sarajevo with water. So that is something that made the people organise themselves. After these units came out with the tanks and the APCs, the organisation idea already started to take root because people could sense that perhaps war was coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the -- during the period of the 4th to the 13th of May, 1992, did anything in particular happen in that area?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: From the 4th to the 13th of May, the most important event was the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. exodus of the population of Dobrinja over -- using the hill of Mojmilo to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Exactly what happened, if you could tell us in that period, from the 4th to the 13th of May?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: After Dobrinja was physically sealed off until about the 10th of May, nothing significant happened. The most significant event in Dobrinja, as I said, was the 13th of May. That's the exodus of the civilian population from Dobrinja towards the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how many people from Dobrinja went towards the city?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but the people that I spoke to assume that, under terrible psychological pressure, some 3 to 5.000 citizens of Dobrinja left to go to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say under what circumstances or why they left?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: That morning, one tank and two APCs appeared on a small bridge that links the banks of the Dobrinja river, which is -- the bridge is right across the part of the settlement that is called Dobrinja IV. They started firing at the neighbourhood from automatic weapons. After that, they used loudspeakers to inform the population that they had the possibility from the morning until 5.00 in the afternoon to leave Dobrinja, and that nothing would happen to them, that they can carry with them only what they were able to carry in their hands, and that members of the army would help them to cross into Sarajevo. Very quickly, a large column of people was formed, women, children, men, with bags in their hands, with clothes, and they were hurrying towards that section of the road held by the at that time, the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that 3 to 5.000 people left. By what route did they leave?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: The route went below the Mojmilo reservoir via the reservoir all the way to the next neighbourhood, that was the Olympic village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Approximately what was the population of Dobrinja at the time when these people left, the 13th, 14th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise number because a lot of the Serb population had already left Dobrinja. But Dobrinja had a population of about 45.000 before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. After these 3 to 5.000 people left, approximately how many people remained in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: We had an authoritative number according to the lists which were required to be given to the international forces in order for humanitarian aid to be given. And this number ranged from 24 to 27.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, following the departure of these people, 3 to 5.000, did anything happen in your community just around the 15th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: These were days full of chaos for the population of Dobrinja, and they were crucial for the survival of Dobrinja. The next day was fairly quiet, but the day after that, the most terrible shelling occurred from all sides of Dobrinja. This was a big surprise for the population. People didn't know what was going on, so they would come out to look at where a shell had landed, but after that, when they could see the consequences, then people started to flee whenever they could, all around the Dobrinja buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say, "people would come out when a shell had landed," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: What I meant to say is that I had the sense that people simply didn't know what war was, and they would come out to see what this looked like, how this was manifested in the location where the shell fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did this have any effect on the rate or level of casualties on the earlier period, earlier period of the conflict when people were unaccustomed to shells falling around them?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said you became the commander of the Dobrinja Brigade. Was that in the Army of the Bosnian Federation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: There was no Federation at that time. There was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since we were under siege, the organisation or the forming of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina proceeded in May and June. We were the last brigade to be formed in the Sarajevo Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe the origins and the formation of the brigade, the Dobrinja Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I was surprised when I was appointed commander of the brigade. I wasn't a military person, and this was a serious and difficult and responsible task. The only thing that I new regarding military matters was what I knew from serving in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For how long did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: When I was called up, the duty lasted for 18 months. But in the army, when I served in 1970 to 71, there were these things that were going on in Croatia the mass movement and the term of duty was shortened to 15 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Forgive me if I say so. But I am trying to move through pretty speedily, but if you could answer the questions I am asking you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, I explain to you. The Prosecution is under certain time limits. So if you give additional information, not specifically asked for, that takes time while the Prosecution might have several other things they are more interested in to know. And if any of the additional things you would like to say specifically is what the Prosecution wants to hear, they will certainly ask you for that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, could you briefly describe for us how the brigade was formed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I found a colonel who lived in Dobrinja and I asked him if he could make up the structure of a brigade, if he could remember what the structure was, and very quickly, he established the brigade. And this is how we began to get organised. So this was the structure of the brigade, based on the recollection of this ex-JNA colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, why did you need to form a unit in Dobrinja at the time, and about when did you and this colonel organise the structure of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, we needed two months in order to get the brigade going in its initial phase of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when was this two months?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: From the 6th of July to -- so July and August. By September, we had already had a formed brigade after a fashion, and this was thanks to the help of this colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, just could you say why it was necessary, in your view, to form a brigade in Dobrinja at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: In the area where we were, the only response to the aggression, which was coming our way, was to unite all the patriotic forces and to respond with a unified system which had already been set up throughout the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the forming of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes Mr. President. Since I never know which aggression we are talking about here, and also I would like to make it a rule, perhaps the witness could be informed about the way that we are treating this word "aggression" before your Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, there would be no misunderstanding as to what the witness meant. Second, the witness was referring to a response to what he called an aggression, which is different from if we are, in general terms, talking about the conflict. Mr. Hadzic, usually, unless there is a specific reason to use words like, "aggression," we usually are talking about the conflict or the armed conflict, since this Chamber has still to make all the determinations necessary. So if you could use a neutral term, please do so. If there is a specific reason why you would use a word like,"defence" or "aggression," please make clear to us why you use that word. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the name of the brigade when it was formed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: The 1st Dobrinja Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did that name remain the same during the conflict or did it change?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: The name changed several times throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let's go to the first two changes. When was the changed first and what was the new name?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was in the first half of 1993, the brigade was called the 5th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And then later, what was it re-named to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know which period this is, but there was a restructuring of the army, and then it was renamed the 125th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the strength of the brigade upon formation, in terms of the amount of men it had?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: At the initial phase, it had from 1.800 to 2000 men. In this first restructuring, then it had about 3.000 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, if you can find a suitable moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn for 20 minutes, so we will adjourn until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, if we could move through quickly, how many battalions did you have in 1992 and 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: In 1992, we had four battalions. In 1993, we had five battalions. And then later on after the restructuring, we had again, four battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic composition of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: 21 per cent were non-Bosniaks and the rest were Bosniaks. About 6 per cent of Croats, the rest were Serbs and there was a small number perhaps 2 Hungarians, a few Romani and then there was one Jew, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About what percentage were Serb?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I think about 13 per cent of the whole number, that is, out of 2000, there were perhaps 200 or so Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on the 29th of October last year, did you mark a map for an OTP investigator which showed certain positions in Dobrinja during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, Your Honours, could the witness be handed Exhibit P3732.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document which you have, Mr. Hadzic, do you see where you have signed and dated the 29th of October 2001?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you have some markings on that map in red ink?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would like you to describe for us what those markings are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you do so, can the map be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have drawn a line from the area of the top of the map where there is the word, "Mojmilo," going down to approximately the middle of the map. What does that line indicate?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: This line indicates the demarcation line or the last line that the brigade was in control of towards Nedzarici and the Airport Settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there any structure or fortification in this area along this line?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mean in the area that we did not have the control of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object in relation to the not very specific term of the word, "structure." It seems to be very vague as definition, the word, "structure."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That line that you have shown us, did you or your brigade construct anything along that line?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: These are our trenches and the area from which we defended ourselves in the event of an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So that is what I am asking you. You said, "these are our trenches." Did you construct trenches along those lines?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Where there is a natural configuration of the ground to dig the trenches where it was easier, we dug trenches and when we -- there were buildings and if they were abandoned then we would make fortifications and then in between buildings, if the ground allowed it, then we created trenches. We had this system of trenches, a network of trenches, and also the buildings that formed our line of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the right-hand side of the map there is a red line which is above the word, "Dobrinja" in italics and below the word, "Novi Grad."

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's our second line, which was the last line that we had under our control towards Lukavica and towards Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And below that line, there is another set of lines going down the map ending above where the word, "Bijelo Polje, is written. Do you see the word "Bijelo Polje," to the right --

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Above that, there are lines. What do those lines depict?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: That is the airport runway and the communication between Kula and Kasindolska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I am asking you about the red line drawn above the word, "Bijelo Polje." What is that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: That is part of our line. In fact, the last line that we had under our control, combination of defence from the buildings, and then we had trenches as much as the ground allowed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is a line ending with a dot and two dashes which comes off that line. Do you see it? Could you point to it please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that dot is just below the word, "Dobrinja." What does that red line indicate?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is part of the trench that we had under our control. Below the school that before the war was called Dusan Pajic-Dasic [Realtime transcript read in error "Dusan"], that's what we had that was under our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the war, was the school functioning?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: No. It was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now there is a line with a circle on it which runs across the airport --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. For the same reasons of usefulness for the cross-examination, it would be good if the school's name is clearly indicated in the transcript. Perhaps spelled, in fact. We only have Dusan, which is the first name. Line 6 of page 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you ask the witness to spell the name of the school, unless it is in his statement, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Of course, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think it is in the statement, however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The school that you just mentioned, what is the name of it and can you spell that name please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Before the war it was called Dusan that is D-U-S-A-N, P-A-J-I-C---D-A-S-I-C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to clarify one issue, Mr. Stamp. The witness was just pointing out a relatively large structure just below the dot. Is that the school or was the school within the red dot? It is a bit unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please tell us which one is the school, the dot or the structure that you are pointing now, below the dot.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: This building is the school, the one that I a indicating right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the record, that is the building below that red dot. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, there is a red line going across what you earlier pointed out the runway. What is that red line demarcating?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: This is the tunnel Dobrinja which was dug from below Dobrinja to the Donji Kotorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the top or the end of the tunnel where it ends at what is shown as the building, could you describe the line from that area to the circle on the line is demarcating?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: From this building I am indicating from the circle, it wasn't a tunnel, it was a trench. And then the entrance to the tunnel is marked with the small red circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have also marked on the map with dots with numbers adjacent to these dots, could you indicate to us what the dot beside the number "1" indicates?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: This point 1 indicates the location where the command of the brigade was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is a dot with a number "2" adjacent to it. What is that indicating?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: This is a place where the Logistics Battalion was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there is a dot with the number "3" beside it. What is that, please?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Also the location where, to start with, this place was also part of the Logistics Battalion. Initially, it was a warehouse storage for the Logistics Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was the Logistics Battalion or -- I withdraw that. When you speak of the Logistics Battalion, are you referring to the headquarters of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: No. I am talking about the support services of the brigade. I am talking about people who cooked for the brigade, cooks, people from the medical services. Those services that support a brigade, in terms of formationally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So when you say that the dot at number "2" indicates a Logistics Battalion, what do you mean? What was located at that dot?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: People from that battalion, that is where the kitchens were and storage warehouses, if we had any food, any equipment. Anything that was necessary to support the brigade for the supplies, for anything for our living conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it from your evidence that at number "2" that was where the Logistics Battalion initially was at?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now in respect to number "3", are you saying that the place housing the Logistics Battalion was divided or that the battalion moved from position number "2" to position number "3"?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I think that this is where the police company was. I think that this number also refers to the police company that was also part of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you are pointing to number "3."

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because all of this location was Logistics Battalion where warehouses and part of the premises were used by the company of the Military Police. This is where they were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You marked on the map with a dot and a number "4" beside it, a particular position. Could you tell us what that position is.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: That's commander of the one of the battalions. I think that was the command of the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you marked on the map a dot with a number "5" beside it. Can you tell us what that is referring to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Command of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you marked on the map a dot with a "6" beside it. Could you tell us what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Command of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said there were four battalions, and you have told us about three. Could you say where the command of the other battalion was located?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: There were three military battalions, one, two, three, and the fourth one was the Logistics Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did your brigade headquarters remain at the same place during 1992, 1993, and 1994, or did it move at any time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: During the conflict, the location of the headquarters changed. The headquarters went to the building marked by "2" for a period of time, and then it moved again closer to number "5" for a period of time, and then again returned to the position number "2" and stayed there until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say, "it moved to a position closer to number '5,'" could you point out exactly where it is that it moved to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Here, right in the middle of this building, there was a middle passage, and there on the right-hand side, there was entrance to former business premises. This is where the headquarters was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you keep the pointer where it is, please. Did you say, and perhaps the record -- or please tell us. Did you say that it moved again closer to number "5" for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us where that was it moved to, when it moved closer to number "5"?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: That was perhaps lower down, two or three entrances to buildings, from this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say it moved closer to position number "5" are you referring to the position number "5" as you have marked on the map in red?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is what you are pointing to just now?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is pointing to position number "2".

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you have a look at -- could you turn the map around because the numbers are upside down. Do you see a number "5" there with a dot beside it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is one of the battalion headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Command of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the brigade headquarters ever move to that place, to that vicinity? Did the brigade headquarters ever move to that place or to that area?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the battalion never came to this location of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction, the headquarters of that brigade never came to that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The lines, as you showed us earlier where the trenches were, did these lines remain in the same position or approximately the same position during the latter part of 1992 through to the summer of 1994 or were there any significant changes in these lines?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: The line remained here throughout the whole of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you referring to all the lines that you have drawn showing the lines of your defences? Did they remain the same during the years 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were there companies which were subordinated to the battalions in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did these companies have headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: The company commands were on the lines that they controlled. There were no commands in the settlements which would be separate. They were directly on the lines. Because the command and control system functioned in the best possible way like that, when the command was together with the men in the trenches or in the areas or buildings which they controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it when you say the company commands, and the lines, you mean the lines of confrontation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Briefly, tell us how well or badly armed you were at the beginning of the conflict, and if and how the situation evolved during the conflict up to the summer of 1994.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: We were extremely poorly equipped, especially at the beginning of the war. And it didn't really improve until the end of the war. So what happened was that supplies for our brigade were not as good as supplies for the other brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did your brigade have mortars or artillery?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1993, we received an 81-millimetre mortar which is between calibres. Because -- so we didn't use it, because we didn't have the shells for it. At the start of assault activities on Treskavica, we received mortars which we used on Treskavica on the locations of Dobrinja. During 1994, we received 60-millimetre mortars, a very small number of them, which we deployed in the battalions, and we used them only in cases of infantry attacks in order to break the infantry, in case they should attack. But we had a few shells for those mortars as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you receive the 60-millimetre mortars, if you could just give us a month and the year?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I think this was in the beginning of 1994, the end of 1993, the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you showed us on that map where your lines of defence were. Beyond those lines going into Dobrinja, were there any other lines of defence?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have indicated to us, on the map, the certain lines which you say were the lines of defence.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, going from those lines, further into Dobrinja itself, were there any other lines of defence?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: No. That was the only line of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was -- having regard to the size of Dobrinja and the population of Dobrinja, was there -- were you able to defend Dobrinja in depth, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: We could defend Dobrinja only along these lines. There was no other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Beyond these trenches, going further into Dobrinja, did -- was anything done or organised for the protection of the population that lived in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Along the depth of Dobrinja there were some communication trenches which were used by the citizens to go from one settlement to the next in order to protect themselves from snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When were these communication trenches built or over what period of time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I think that at the beginning of the war, maybe in 1993, I think that this was done. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In order to protect the civilians, you spoke of sniping. Did you do anything else apart from building trenches, communication trenches?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Wherever we were able to use anything to protect people from getting killed, we would do it. For example, we couldn't dig across rivers or bridges so we would fill containers with earth and we would place them on the edges, like a fence, so the citizens would be able to cross from one side of the river to the other. Or we would place trucks from Dobrinja V practically all the way to the health centre to Mojmilo. These trucks were full of cement. We would place them one behind the other in order to protect Dobrinja from sniper activities from sniper nests in Nedzarici and from the theological -- the Faculty of Theology. Even later when we received foil from the international forces to protect roofs that were damaged, we would place this foil in some areas in order to create a kind of protective curtain from sniper activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there a Civil Defence organised in Dobrinja during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not right from the beginning, but it was established later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may just go back a little bit. Did your soldiers fire from these communications trenches which you say were in the depths of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the relation of the Civil Defence organisation to the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you may get that map, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you describe the relationship please. Was the Civil Defence under the command of the army or was it separate or the same organisation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: It was separate. It wasn't under the military command. So I repeat, it had a separate command. We didn't have command over it, but we did help them. Because they had a lot of duties, so when they lacked the manpower, we would provide our manpower for them, so they could accomplish the tasks that they were supposed to accomplish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were the tasks and duties of the Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: To provide the removal of garbage in Dobrinja, to try to ensure water supply, they created improvised ovens or stoves for cooking because there was no fuel. They would assist in placing the wounded into hospital. Also, they took care that they had food. So these were the tasks that the civil protection would carry out anywhere else. Civil protection even had a group of people who were acting as firefighters and they went out to put out fires wherever they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the Civil Defence have role in constructing or building any of the structures that you mentioned for the protection of civilians?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I said that they dug these special pits where garbage was deposited, in order to prevent outbreaks of infectious diseases. Also, we were digging wells in order to get supplies of drinking water because drinking water was one of the biggest problems for the normal life in Dobrinja. The civil protection also organised from building to building, kindergartens. Also it organised elementary and secondary schools so that they could start working in the central parts of the settlement. The opening of school for art, a press centre, a cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that there was sniping going on and efforts had to be made to protect the population from sniping. Did the civilian defence play a part in these efforts to protect the population from sniping?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Since members of the civil protection were usually elderly people or people unfit for military service, if somebody was hit, they wouldn't be the ones to pull that person out. This was usually done by soldiers. They wouldn't send people like that to carry out things like that, if a person was killed or died. The civil protection then took care about organising the funerals of those people, their burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, may I recall and show the witness Exhibit D85. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so. Would you also keep in mind, I don't know how much time you would need, that we need some time for procedural issues, and I think I said the last 15 minutes. If it is a matter of one or two minutes, fine. Otherwise, perhaps we should have a break. Not a break but we should interrupt the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would probably spend about 5 or more minutes on this document. I don't know if it would be worthwhile proceeding with it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, we better first interrupt the examination of the witness. Mr. Hadzic, since we have a few procedural issues to discuss, and since we have to stop at 7.00, we have to interrupt your examination now. But it will continue tomorrow. So would you please not talk to anyone about the testimony that you gave in this court, and would you please come back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the same courtroom. Yes. Mr. Usher, would you then please escort Mr. Hadzic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, or Ms. Pilipovic. I don't know who to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had put a few questions to you, you would still inform the Chamber about the witnesses, the presentation of the Defence case and we had another outstanding issue. Could you please inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Ms. Pilipovic is better suited for this -- these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence, since we are continuously here in The Hague and the proceedings are being conducted every day, in principle, the Defence would first of all like to say that it will have 7 expert witnesses. We were planning 55 work hours. Now, I am speaking in general lines. 55 work hours in order to examine them. So according to our estimates, that is 12 working days. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, you are talking about the time the Defence would need to examine the witnesses, not to --.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So that is an average of 7 and a half hours of each expert witness? 7 expert witnesses, 55 hours according to my arithmetics, it's even a bit over-

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps my calculations are -- I need to recheck them. But the Defence estimates that the examination of our military analyst and strategist will probably take at least 5 or 6 working days. Perhaps this is where the discrepancy comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then the average becomes even if the others will take not much time. Would that mean that no, you do not intend to present a report of expert witnesses, which is the usual way of doing it under 94 bis?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will present the findings of the experts but the Defence would like to examine each of the Defence experts, particularly the military analyst and strategist, and also the expert for shelling and artillery, as well as the ballistics expert, the forensic medicine experts, as well as the experts who will talk about artillery weapons, the firing weapons. And also, one who will discuss the medical evidence or documents which have already been adopted, admitted into evidence. So if you would like, I could specify the time in general lines for each of these experts, if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I understand you well, so that is 55 hours, there are the 7 expert witnesses, and then --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, may I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. When we are talking about witnesses, at present, the Defence estimates that we need to call 93 witnesses. The Defence plans on average to spend two hours per witness, two hours and 30 minutes per witness. If my calculations are correct, 93 witnesses at two and a half hours each, this comes to 240 hours or 60 working days. The 12 working days that will be necessary to examine the experts, plus the 60 days, that would come to 72 working days, roughly. Then we will also probably examine some witnesses via videolink, and right now we are not able to predict evidence in accordance with Rule 92 bis. So when we are talking about the videolink and 92 bis, the Defence estimates roughly that this could take up more time. So we might need more than the 72 working days, due to technical difficulties, for example, when we are talking about the videolink, and then also when we are talking about Rule 92 bis, we don't know whether the Prosecution would like to cross-examine such witnesses and we are calculating here also our time which is necessary for the opening or the introductory questioning. We will also have a large number of documents and maps to be tendered into evidence, particularly through the experts. And that is why, when we were making our estimates about this 55 hours and 12 working days, this is our estimate that applies to the military expert and the expert for the shelling, the artillery and ballistics. Then we will also have an expert who will be a psychiatrist. He will talk about fear. We will have an expert who will talk about the causes of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But, once again, I would like to say that if we need to specify our time requirements in more detail, we can do that. But this is just a rough estimate of the time we will need in view -- having in mind the fact that we have spent the past 7 months here in The Hague, that proceedings were conducted every day. So this makes it more difficult for the Defence to communicate with other members of our team in order to arrive at a more precise estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just ask you a few questions. You tell the Chamber that you would need, apart from the possible experts you just mentioned for witnesses, 60 working days in court, 12 days for the experts. That makes 72 days in court. And that is just the time the Defence would need. So if we would have a situation where the Prosecution -- let's just assume that the Prosecution does what the Defence has done, that is, to make more time than the examination-in-chief for cross-examination, that would be -- well, let's just assume that that will take just as much time as the Defence did, that makes 144 days. And let's just assume that the parties are just as efficient as they have been during the presentation of the Prosecution case. That means that the time used for examining witnesses is approximately, well, let's say, 75 per cent. So you should add one-third to 144 days. That would mean approximately 48 days. That would then make 192 days for the Defence, where we are now at day 121 for the Prosecution. That would mean approximately half extra compared to the Prosecutions' case, where if you would look at the statistics, you would find that Defence case, the presentation of the Defence cases, on average, takes approximately 70 per cent of the time of the presentation of the Prosecution case. I am just trying to understand and to think over the arethmetical part of what you are telling us, just in order to know for sure that I do understand the Defence well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I entirely understand what you have just said, and I did say that this was a rough schedule. In view of the time and the percentages that you have given us now, I am trying right now in my head to give you some kind of response. I will analyse all that we have heard right now, and if you permit us a little bit more time, we will reconsider and then state our position. But I would like to repeat again, that this is a rough schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I am not asking for much details. But I am just pointing out to you where the examination-in-chief of the Prosecution took, until now, and, of course, we have still approximately 10 days to go, some 160 hours. And on the rough schedule you are presenting, you are quite close to 300 hours, which is approximately double of the time. Well, I am just trying to add 55 hours for the experts and 240 hours roughly for 93 witnesses, as you indicated for 2 hours and 30 minutes for each witness. But, okay, at least I do understand. Are there any other -- is there any -- has the Defence any idea as to when we are talking about witnesses, what type of witnesses. As you might have noticed, the Prosecution has split up its witnesses in certain categories, like sniping incident witnesses. Or do you have a similar, I mean, among these 93 witnesses, is there any categorisation made?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witnesses have not yet been put into categories. So when we are talking about categorising witnesses, the Defence would request enough time so that we could provide you this information this week, which witnesses would testify to which matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was this the rough schedule you wanted to provide or are there any other elements that you have not mentioned yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a rough schedule that I have just given.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what we did not mention, and I believe that it is important to state it now, is that we had the impression that the Defence would have a lot of trouble to keep up the rhythm of five days per week, five working days a week, which we have done so far quite valiantly. Because I think we will need some time to present the Defence case, time to prepare. I will be ready to present this in an oral argument whenever you wish me to do so, but I think it is important to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I know that most of the time was given to the Defence. If you have any observations to make, any submissions please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President. I notice that the outline does not include the accused and I assume he would take some days in chief and certainly he would take many days in cross-examination. I think that is important for time estimates. Secondly, Mr. President I would be grateful if we could receive before, well, as soon as possible, some idea of the timetable that will operate in terms of no case to answer and should we get so far, in particular, the names of the witnesses that the Defence proposes to call and the 65 ter summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I give you and perhaps the most important part some guidance, and that is what will happen with a -- if the Defence would file a no case to answer motion. The -- I think we indicated already or I don't know whether we did or not. But the three weeks recess should be respected. I think everyone needs that. We have been sitting in court five days a week. So that would mean that the -- if the Prosecution concludes its case the second of August, then we would first have three weeks of recess, and then there would be one week for the Defence to file a motion of no case to answer. The Chamber considers it reasonable if the Defence would then file its response in two weeks' time, and that the Chamber assumes that it could take a decision in two weeks' time as well. So altogether, five weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a point of clarification. You said the Chamber considers it reasonable if the Defence would then file its response in two weeks' time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it should be the Prosecution. Speaking to yourself is sometimes useful, but that is not what I intended to say. So in general terms, I would say on from late August, that would be five weeks, that would also mean that if this schedule would be followed, that the Defence would start its case, I think, the last Monday in the month of September, which would be, I am not quite sure, but it is 29th or the 30th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That would still leave the issue of the date by which the Prosecution is to receive the list of witnesses and also the list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will give you an answer to that on very short notice. Yes. I think that we have to adjourn now until tomorrow. The Chamber thanks the Defence for giving its first rough estimate of what time it would take to present its case. We will adjourn until tomorrow, a quarter past 2.00.
